client: I've been really stressed out lately because I failed two exams this semester, and now I keep spiraling about whether I'm even going to be able to graduate on time. It's like this constant knot in my stomach that won't go away, no matter what I do. Honestly, I'm not sure talking about it is going to change my GPA or fix anything, but I figured I had to try something.
therapist: That constant knot in your stomach sounds really exhausting, and it makes complete sense that failing two exams would send your mind into overdrive about the bigger picture of graduating. I also notice you came here even while doubting it would help — that actually takes a lot of courage, and it tells me a part of you is still looking for a way through this. Can you tell me a little more about what that spiraling looks like for you — what kinds of thoughts tend to show up most?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It's like my brain just runs this loop where I think, "If I failed these two, I'm probably going to fail the next ones too, and then I'll have to retake courses, and then I won't graduate with my friends, and then my whole future is ruined." It sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels completely real and unstoppable. And then I start feeling guilty on top of it, like I should have studied harder or been smarter about managing my time, which just makes everything worse.
therapist: What you're describing has a name in CBT — it's called "catastrophic thinking," and the fact that you can already notice it sounds dramatic when you say it out loud is actually a really important first step, because it means part of you can observe the loop rather than just being swept away by it. That guilt layered on top is so common but so cruel, because it takes an already hard situation and adds a second wave of pain. I'm curious — when that loop starts running, is there anything that's ever helped you hit even a small pause on it, even briefly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, sometimes putting on music or going for a walk helps for like twenty minutes, but then the thoughts just come rushing back the second I stop moving or the song ends. It's like I can distract myself but I can't actually make the thoughts go away, so it feels kind of pointless in the long run. I guess I'm skeptical that there's anything that actually stops it rather than just temporarily muting it.
therapist: The way you're describing this — almost quietly resigned to it — makes me wonder if underneath the skepticism there's also something that feels a little defeated or worn down, like you've been carrying this longer than just these two exams. You're right that distraction isn't a cure, but what you're actually doing with music and walking is giving your nervous system a real, if brief, reprieve — and that's not nothing, it's actually a clue about what your mind needs. What do you think would feel different about a thought *actually losing its grip* versus just being muted — what would that even look like for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think if a thought actually lost its grip, I'd be able to look at the situation and feel like it's manageable rather than catastrophic, like I could acknowledge I failed the exams without it automatically meaning my entire future is falling apart. But honestly I'm not even sure I believe that's possible for me right now, because the thought feels so tied to reality, like it's not just anxiety making things up, I actually did fail two exams and that's a real problem. So I guess I'm not sure how to separate what's catastrophic thinking from what's just... legitimate concern.
therapist: You've actually just landed on one of the most important distinctions in CBT — the difference between a real problem and a catastrophic interpretation of it, and you're right that both can be true at once: failing two exams *is* a real concern *and* "my entire future is ruined" is your anxious mind extrapolating far beyond what the facts actually support. The goal isn't to pretend the exams didn't happen, but to hold the real problem at its actual size rather than letting anxiety inflate it into something that swallows everything. What do you think the situation would look like if you described it as accurately as possible — just the facts, without the spiral attached?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, so just the facts... I failed two exams, which means my grades in those courses took a hit, and I might need to do really well on the finals or talk to my professors about options. That actually does sound less terrifying when I say it that way, but I'm worried that's just because I'm sitting here in a calm environment talking to you, and the second I'm back in my apartment alone at night it's going to inflate right back into the catastrophic version. How do I hold onto that more accurate framing when I'm not in a controlled setting like this?
therapist: What you just did — reframing the situation into its actual facts — is exactly the skill, and you're already doing it, which matters more than it might feel like right now. One way to hold onto it when you're alone is to literally write down that grounded version in your own words and keep it somewhere accessible, so when the spiral starts at night you have something concrete to return to rather than trying to reconstruct it from scratch in the middle of anxiety. Would it feel doable to try that this week — maybe even just a few sentences you could read back to yourself when the loop starts?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I can try that, but I'm a little doubtful that reading a few sentences is going to feel convincing when I'm already deep in the spiral, because in those moments the catastrophic version feels so much more real and urgent than any calm reframe I wrote down earlier. It's like I'm worried I'll read it and just think "yeah but that was before I really thought it through, the situation actually IS that bad." I guess my question is, how do I make myself actually believe it in the moment rather than just reading words that feel hollow?
therapist: That's such a sharp and honest observation — your anxious brain is essentially pre-debunking the tool before you even use it, which is itself a form of the spiral. The key is that the goal of the written reframe isn't to out-argue the anxiety in the moment, but to act as an anchor that interrupts the loop just long enough for you to ask one small question: "What's the actual next step I can take?" — because anxiety loses some of its power when you shift from "what does this mean about my future" to "what's one concrete thing I can do tomorrow, like emailing a professor." Does that feel like a more workable entry point than trying to convince yourself the catastrophe isn't real?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually does feel a little more workable, because it's less about winning an argument with my own brain and more about just doing something small and concrete. But I'm realizing that even thinking about emailing my professor makes me anxious in a different way, like I'm scared of what they might say or that they'll think I'm making excuses. I guess the spiral has more branches than I realized.
therapist: It sounds like you're making a really meaningful discovery — that the anxiety isn't just one loop but a whole network of them, and the fear of judgment from your professor is its own tender spot worth paying attention to. That worry that you'll be seen as making excuses tells me something about how you're seeing yourself right now, like you need to have a perfect reason to deserve help. What do you think your professor is actually more likely to think — that you're making excuses, or that you're a student trying to figure out a hard situation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Rationally, I know most professors have probably seen struggling students before and aren't sitting there waiting to judge me, but emotionally it still feels like I'd be exposing myself as someone who couldn't handle things. I think part of me believes that if I was really capable, I wouldn't need to ask for help in the first place, so reaching out almost feels like confirming my worst fears about myself. It's uncomfortable to realize that the anxiety about the exams and the anxiety about asking for help might both be coming from the same place.
therapist: What you just connected is really profound — that belief that "needing help means I'm not capable" is often at the root of so much anxiety, because it turns every struggle into evidence of a fundamental flaw rather than just a hard moment. That's a really painful way to move through the world, and it makes sense that reaching out feels exposing when asking for help has become wrapped up in your sense of worth. Where do you think that belief came from — has needing help always felt like a sign of weakness to you, or is that something that developed over time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it developed over time, honestly. Growing up, the message I got was that you figure things out yourself and you don't burden other people, so I learned pretty early that struggling was something you kept quiet and pushed through. It's strange to sit here and realize that something I thought was just being self-sufficient might actually be making everything harder, including this whole exam situation.
therapist: What you just named takes real courage to see — that something you were taught as a strength, self-sufficiency, has quietly been working against you by making every moment of struggle feel like something shameful to hide. There's something that sounds both relieving and a little sad in what you're saying, like you're meeting a younger version of yourself who learned to carry things alone and did the best they could with what they were taught. How does it feel to consider that asking for help — from your professor, or even being here today — might actually be a sign of capability rather than a lack of it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: It feels weird to hear that framed as capability, because it's so opposite to how I've always thought about it, but there's something about it that I want to believe even if I'm not fully there yet. I think the relieving and sad thing you said is accurate, like there's a part of me that feels a little sorry for how hard I've been on myself without even realizing it. I'm just not sure how you change a belief that's been baked in for that long, because it's not like I can just decide to see it differently overnight.
therapist: That compassion you're starting to feel for yourself — even just a flicker of it — is actually the beginning of how beliefs like this do shift, not through a single decision but through small moments of catching yourself and gently offering a different interpretation. You don't have to fully believe it yet; you just said "there's a part of me that wants to," and that part is worth listening to and nurturing. What might it look like to treat yourself this week with even a fraction of the understanding you'd offer a close friend who was in your exact situation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
